summary: The right heart pumps its whole output through the lungs, and the left heart receives it back, so the two organs work as one circuit. Exam items test how the pulmonary circulation differs from the systemic one, how breathing changes venous return, and how disease in one organ overloads the other.

points: Right and left ventricular outputs are equal over time (about 5 L/min at rest).
Pulmonary artery pressure is about 25/8 mmHg (mean about 15 mmHg); systemic is about 120/80 mmHg.
Pulmonary vascular resistance is much lower than systemic, roughly one tenth.
Pulmonary capillary pressure is about 7 mmHg, which keeps fluid out of the alveoli.
Bronchial arteries (systemic) feed the airways; part of their venous blood drains into pulmonary veins, a small normal shunt.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: low alveolar O2 constricts nearby arterioles and sends blood to better ventilated alveoli.
Systemic arterioles do the opposite and dilate in hypoxia.
Chronic global hypoxia (COPD, high altitude) constricts vessels throughout the lung and causes pulmonary hypertension.
When cardiac output rises, closed capillaries open (recruitment) and open ones widen (distension), so resistance falls.
Resistance is lowest near FRC; at high lung volume alveolar vessels are stretched and compressed, at low volume extra-alveolar vessels narrow.

notes.h: Gravity and the zones of the lung
points: Upright, the base gets more blood flow and more ventilation than the apex; flow rises more steeply.
V/Q is about 3 at the apex and about 0.6 at the base; the whole-lung average is about 0.8.
Zone 1 (no flow) is normally absent; it appears with low arterial pressure (hemorrhage) or high alveolar pressure (positive pressure ventilation).
Inspiration lowers intrathoracic pressure, raises venous return to the right heart, and raises right ventricular stroke volume.
At the same time pulmonary veins hold more blood, so left ventricular filling and systolic pressure dip slightly (under 10 mmHg).
A drop over 10 mmHg is pulsus paradoxus: cardiac tamponade, severe asthma, or COPD.
Inspiration delays pulmonic valve closure, which gives normal (physiologic) splitting of S2.
Positive pressure ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, lowers venous return, and can lower cardiac output.

notes.h: When one organ fails, the other is loaded
points: Left heart failure or mitral stenosis raises left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressure and causes pulmonary edema.
Alveolar edema appears once pulmonary capillary pressure exceeds plasma colloid osmotic pressure (about 28 mmHg).
Chronic lung disease or hypoxia raises pulmonary artery pressure and causes right ventricular hypertrophy and failure (cor pulmonale).
A large pulmonary embolus suddenly raises right ventricular afterload (acute cor pulmonale).
A right-to-left shunt sends venous blood past the lungs, so hypoxemia barely improves with 100% O2.

notes.h: The lung as a metabolic organ
points: ACE on pulmonary capillary endothelium converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
The same enzyme inactivates bradykinin.
The pulmonary capillary bed filters small clots and debris from venous blood before it reaches the systemic arteries.

tricks.label: Hypoxia flips in the lung
tricks.text: Everywhere else, low O2 dilates arterioles to bring in more blood. In the lung, low O2 constricts them so blood goes where the air is.

tricks.label: Alveolar pressure walks down the line
tricks.text: Write arterial, venous, alveolar. Zone 1 puts alveolar first, zone 2 puts it second, zone 3 puts it last.

tricks.label: The 100% O2 test
tricks.text: If extra oxygen fixes the hypoxemia, think V/Q mismatch or diffusion. If it barely helps, think shunt.

highYield: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is the main local control of pulmonary blood flow.
Chronic hypoxic lung disease leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
V/Q is highest at the apex and lowest at the base.
Inspiration raises right heart filling and splits S2.
Pulsus paradoxus over 10 mmHg points to cardiac tamponade or severe obstructive lung disease.
Pulmonary ACE makes angiotensin II and breaks down bradykinin.
A right-to-left shunt causes hypoxemia that 100% O2 barely corrects.
pitfalls: Cor pulmonale means right heart disease caused by lung disease or pulmonary vessels; right heart failure from left heart failure does not count.
Pulmonary embolism is a dead-space (high V/Q) problem in the blocked area, yet hypoxemia comes from low V/Q in the overperfused areas.
Both blood flow and ventilation are greater at the base; V/Q is lower there because flow increases more than ventilation.

l: Zone 1: alveolar > arterial > venous, no flow
Zone 2: arterial > alveolar > venous, flow set by arterial minus alveolar pressure
Zone 3: arterial > venous > alveolar, continuous flow
Zone 1 normally absent; appears with hemorrhage or positive pressure ventilation
V/Q about 3 at apex
V/Q about 0.6 at base
Flow and ventilation both rise toward the base, flow more steeply

summary: Many heart and vessel diseases are driven by the immune system: atherosclerosis is chronic inflammation, rheumatic fever is molecular mimicry, and most vasculitis is antibody, immune complex, or T-cell injury. The exam asks you to match each disease to its hypersensitivity type and immune cell.

points: Injured endothelium expresses VCAM-1 and recruits monocytes and T cells into the intima.
LDL trapped in the intima is oxidized; macrophages take it up through scavenger receptors and become foam cells.
Scavenger receptors are not shut off by cell cholesterol, so foam cells keep filling.
Cholesterol crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome, which releases IL-1 beta.
Th1 cells release IFN-gamma, which activates macrophages; PDGF draws smooth muscle cells in to build the fibrous cap.
Macrophage metalloproteinases thin the cap and make the plaque prone to rupture.
C-reactive protein (hs-CRP) is a liver-made marker of this inflammation and predicts cardiac risk.
Follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 2 to 3 weeks.
Antibodies and T cells against the streptococcal M protein cross-react with heart antigens such as cardiac myosin.
Review books classify it as type II hypersensitivity; CD4 T cells also drive the valve damage.
Acute lesion: Aschoff bodies with Anitschkow (caterpillar) cells; pancarditis.
ASO and anti-DNase B titers show the recent strep infection.
Immune complex (type III): polyarteritis nodosa (often hepatitis B), IgA vasculitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (hepatitis C), lupus vasculitis.
ANCA-associated (few immune deposits): granulomatosis with polyangiitis (PR3, c-ANCA), microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (MPO, p-ANCA).
ANCA bind neutrophil enzymes on primed neutrophils and trigger degranulation that injures the vessel wall.
Anti-GBM disease is type II: antibodies to type IV collagen in glomerular and alveolar basement membranes.
T-cell granulomatous arteritis (type IV): giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis.
Hyperacute: preformed antibodies (ABO or HLA) bind graft endothelium within minutes, causing thrombosis.
Acute cellular: CD8 and CD4 T cells attack the myocardium, weeks to months after transplant.
Acute antibody-mediated: antibodies to donor HLA injure graft vessels.
Chronic: cardiac allograft vasculopathy, a diffuse concentric intimal thickening of coronary arteries.
Viral myocarditis: direct viral injury, then a T-cell response that can lead to dilated cardiomyopathy.
Hypersensitivity myocarditis: drug reaction with eosinophils in the myocardium.
Dressler syndrome: autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI, against myocardial antigens released by necrosis.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis in lupus: sterile vegetations on both sides of the valve, usually mitral.
Maternal anti-Ro (SSA) antibodies cross the placenta and cause congenital heart block.
Rare myocarditis after mRNA COVID-19 vaccines, mostly in young males within days of a dose.

tricks.label: ACID
tricks.text: Hypersensitivity types I to IV: Anaphylactic and Atopic (I), Cytotoxic antibody-mediated (II), Immune complex (III), Delayed cell-mediated (IV).

tricks.label: Throat vs skin
tricks.text: Rheumatic fever follows strep throat only. Poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis can follow throat or skin infection.

tricks.label: Rejection clock
tricks.text: Minutes means preformed antibody, weeks means T cells, years means vessel narrowing.

highYield: Rheumatic fever: M protein antibodies cross-react with cardiac myosin (molecular mimicry).
Aschoff bodies are the hallmark of acute rheumatic carditis.
Foam cells form through scavenger receptor uptake of oxidized LDL.
Polyarteritis nodosa is linked to hepatitis B and spares the lungs.
c-ANCA (PR3) points to granulomatosis with polyangiitis; p-ANCA (MPO) to microscopic polyangiitis or EGPA.
Chronic heart transplant rejection appears as accelerated coronary artery narrowing.
Maternal anti-Ro antibodies cause neonatal complete heart block.
pitfalls: Rheumatic fever vegetations are small and sterile along the closure line; infective endocarditis vegetations are large, bulky, and contain organisms.
Dressler syndrome comes weeks after MI and is autoimmune; fibrinous pericarditis in the first few days comes from the necrosis itself.
ANCA vasculitis is called pauci-immune because few immune deposits are seen, which separates it from immune complex vasculitis.

Type II: IgG or IgM against fixed antigens

Type III: immune complexes deposit in vessel walls
Type III examples: polyarteritis nodosa, IgA vasculitis, serum sickness
Type IV: T cells and macrophages
Type IV examples: acute cellular rejection, giant cell arteritis

Monocytes enter the intima and become macrophages
LDL is oxidized in the intima
Scavenger receptor uptake makes foam cells

summary: This unit covers the organisms behind the listed cardiovascular infections: the bacteria of infective endocarditis, Trypanosoma cruzi, Borrelia burgdorferi, Rickettsia rickettsii, the hemorrhagic fever viruses, and the myocarditis viruses. Questions pair each organism with its shape, vector, life cycle, and the virulence factor that explains the disease.

points: Staphylococcus aureus: gram-positive cocci in clusters, catalase and coagulase positive; acute endocarditis on normal valves and in IV drug use.
S. aureus virulence: protein A binds the Fc end of IgG; clumping factor and fibronectin-binding proteins help it stick to valves.
Viridans streptococci: alpha-hemolytic, optochin resistant; subacute endocarditis on damaged valves after dental work.
Viridans strep make dextran, which binds fibrin-platelet clumps on damaged valves.
Enterococcus faecalis: grows in 6.5% NaCl and bile; endocarditis after GI or GU procedures.
Staphylococcus epidermidis: coagulase negative, makes biofilm on prosthetic valves and devices.
Streptococcus gallolyticus (formerly S. bovis) endocarditis is linked to colon cancer.
Flagellated protozoan; spread by triatomine (reduviid, kissing) bugs in Latin America.
The bug defecates while feeding; trypomastigotes in the feces enter the bite wound or the conjunctiva (Romana sign).
Also spread by blood transfusion, organ transplant, mother to fetus, and contaminated food.
Trypomastigotes circulate in blood and do not divide; amastigotes multiply inside heart muscle, smooth muscle, and macrophages.
Chronic disease years later: dilated cardiomyopathy with apical aneurysm and conduction block, megaesophagus, and megacolon.
Spirochete; stains poorly with Gram stain, seen with Giemsa or Wright stain.
Vector: Ixodes ticks (black-legged deer tick); white-footed mouse is the main reservoir; deer feed the adult ticks.
Transmission usually needs about 36 to 48 hours of tick attachment.
Switches outer surface proteins: OspA in the tick gut, OspC when it moves to the host.
Antigenic variation of the VlsE surface protein helps it avoid antibodies.
Unusual genome: a linear chromosome plus many linear and circular plasmids.
Lyme carditis (early disseminated stage) causes AV block of varying degree.
Small gram-negative obligate intracellular bacterium; cannot make enough of its own CoA and NAD+.
Vector: Dermacentor ticks (American dog tick, Rocky Mountain wood tick); most US cases are in the southeast and south-central states.
Infects vascular endothelial cells and spreads cell to cell using host actin.
Endothelial infection causes vasculitis, leaky vessels, edema, low blood pressure, and thrombocytopenia.
Rash starts on wrists and ankles, spreads to the trunk, and involves palms and soles.
Yellow fever and dengue: flaviviruses (enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA), spread by Aedes aegypti mosquitoes.
Yellow fever damages hepatocytes (Councilman bodies) and causes jaundice and bleeding; a live attenuated vaccine prevents it.
Dengue has four serotypes; a second infection with a different serotype raises the risk of severe dengue through antibody-dependent enhancement.
Ebola and Marburg: filoviruses (enveloped, filamentous, negative-sense single-stranded RNA); fruit bats are the likely reservoir; people spread it through body fluids.
Filoviruses infect macrophages, dendritic cells, and endothelium; Ebola VP35 blocks type I interferon.
Common end path: endothelial leak, cytokine storm, and consumptive coagulopathy (DIC).
Coxsackie B virus (enterovirus, picornavirus family) is the classic cause; spread mainly fecal-oral.
Coxsackie B enters cardiomyocytes through the coxsackie-adenovirus receptor (CAR); its protease 2A cleaves dystrophin.
Adenovirus uses the same CAR receptor and is common in children.
Parvovirus B19 and HHV-6 are now frequently found in heart biopsies; parvovirus infects endothelial cells.

tricks.label: HACEK
tricks.text: Haemophilus, Aggregatibacter (formerly Actinobacillus), Cardiobacterium, Eikenella, Kingella: fastidious gram-negative causes of culture-negative endocarditis.

tricks.label: Match the procedure to the bug
tricks.text: Dental work brings viridans strep. GI or GU procedures bring Enterococcus. A new prosthetic valve brings S. epidermidis. IV drug use brings S. aureus to the tricuspid valve.

tricks.label: RMSF rash travels inward
tricks.text: Rocky Mountain spotted fever starts at the wrists and ankles and moves to the trunk. Typhus rash does the reverse, starting on the trunk.

highYield: S. aureus is the most common cause of acute endocarditis and of endocarditis in IV drug users.
Viridans strep dextran lets it stick to fibrin-platelet clumps on damaged valves.
S. gallolyticus endocarditis calls for a colonoscopy to look for colon cancer.
Chagas disease: triatomine bug, Latin America, dilated cardiomyopathy plus megaesophagus and megacolon.
Lyme carditis presents as AV block.
R. rickettsii infects endothelium and causes a vasculitis with a rash on palms and soles.
Dengue: secondary infection with a different serotype causes severe disease through antibody-dependent enhancement.
Coxsackie B is the classic cause of viral myocarditis and pericarditis.
pitfalls: Viridans strep and S. pneumoniae are both alpha-hemolytic; S. pneumoniae is optochin sensitive and bile soluble, viridans strep is neither.
Ixodes ticks carry Borrelia; Dermacentor ticks carry Rickettsia rickettsii.
Despite the name, most RMSF cases in the US occur in the southeast and south-central states.
Flaviviruses (yellow fever, dengue) are positive-sense RNA; filoviruses (Ebola, Marburg) are negative-sense RNA.

Inside host cells they become amastigotes and divide
Cells burst and release trypomastigotes into the blood
A bug takes up trypomastigotes in a blood meal
In the bug gut they become epimastigotes and multiply
Target tissues: heart muscle, GI smooth muscle and nerve plexus

summary: Systemic hypertension loads the left ventricle and damages arterioles in the brain, kidney, retina, and heart. Pulmonary hypertension loads the right ventricle and ends in right heart failure. Know the definitions, the main causes, the vessel changes, and the organ damage for each.

points: ACC/AHA 2017: stage 1 is 130 to 139 or 80 to 89 mmHg; stage 2 is 140/90 mmHg or higher.
Primary (essential) hypertension is about 90 to 95% of cases; it is polygenic with environmental triggers.
Risk factors: older age, family history, obesity, high sodium intake, excess alcohol, inactivity, diabetes.
Secondary causes: renal artery stenosis, kidney disease, primary aldosteronism, pheochromocytoma, Cushing syndrome, coarctation, sleep apnea.
Renal artery stenosis: atherosclerosis in older adults, fibromuscular dysplasia in younger women.

notes.h: Systemic hypertension: vessel and heart changes
points: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis: pink glassy arteriole walls from plasma protein leak; seen in chronic hypertension and diabetes.
Hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis: onion-skin wall layers, often with fibrinoid necrosis, in severe (malignant) hypertension.
Pressure overload causes concentric left ventricular hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in parallel).
The thick, stiff ventricle fills poorly (diastolic dysfunction), enlarging the left atrium and raising the risk of atrial fibrillation.
Hypertensive emergency: severe pressure (often 180/120 mmHg or higher) with acute organ damage.
Mean pulmonary artery pressure over 20 mmHg at rest by right heart catheterization (older cutoff 25 mmHg).
Left heart disease (group 2) is the most common cause.
Pulmonary arterial hypertension (group 1) includes idiopathic, heritable (BMPR2), drug-related, connective tissue disease, HIV, and portal hypertension.
BMPR2 loss-of-function mutations allow smooth muscle proliferation in small pulmonary arteries.
Endothelial imbalance: low NO and prostacyclin, high endothelin-1.
Medial hypertrophy and intimal fibrosis of small arteries; plexiform lesions in severe pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Atherosclerosis can appear in the large pulmonary arteries.
Symptoms: exertional dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, syncope.
Signs: loud P2, right ventricular heave, tricuspid regurgitation murmur, raised jugular venous pressure, edema.
ECG: right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy.
Systemic: stroke (including intracerebral hemorrhage from Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms), coronary disease and MI, heart failure.
Systemic: aortic dissection, abdominal aortic aneurysm, chronic kidney disease (nephrosclerosis), retinopathy.
Pulmonary: right ventricular hypertrophy and failure (cor pulmonale), arrhythmias, sudden death.

tricks.label: Concentric means pressure
tricks.text: Pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) thickens the wall inward. Volume overload (regurgitation) stretches the chamber outward, which is eccentric hypertrophy.

tricks.label: Order of PH groups
tricks.text: List the groups in order: 1 disease of the pulmonary arteries themselves, 2 left heart disease, 3 lung disease or hypoxia, 4 clots blocking the arteries, 5 everything else. Group 2 is the most common.

tricks.label: Onion skin means emergency
tricks.text: Hyaline arterioles mean long, mild pressure. Onion-skin arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis mean malignant hypertension.

highYield: Essential hypertension makes up about 90 to 95% of cases.
Primary aldosteronism is the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension: high blood pressure, high aldosterone, low renin, and sometimes low potassium.
Hypertension is the main risk factor for aortic dissection and intracerebral hemorrhage.
Concentric LVH is the heart's response to chronic pressure overload.
BMPR2 mutations cause heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Plexiform lesions mark severe pulmonary arterial hypertension.
The most common cause of pulmonary hypertension is left heart disease.
pitfalls: Cor pulmonale is right heart disease from lung or pulmonary vascular disease; pulmonary hypertension from left heart failure is group 2.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis appears in both hypertension and diabetes; onion-skin change points to malignant hypertension.
Fibromuscular dysplasia (young women, string of beads) and atherosclerosis (older adults, ostial narrowing) both cause renal artery stenosis.

dumps.p: Draw a body outline. Mark every organ that long-term systemic hypertension damages, and write the lesion found in each.
l: Brain: ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage (Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms)
Eye: retinopathy with AV nicking, hemorrhages, cotton wool spots; papilledema if malignant
Heart: concentric LVH, diastolic dysfunction, coronary disease
Aorta: dissection and aneurysm
Kidney: hyaline arteriolosclerosis and nephrosclerosis
Malignant hypertension: hyperplastic arteriolosclerosis with fibrinoid necrosis
Peripheral arteries: atherosclerosis and PAD

dumps.p: Trace how pulmonary arterial hypertension leads to right heart failure, starting with a BMPR2 mutation.
l: BMPR2 loss of function
Endothelial imbalance: less NO and prostacyclin, more endothelin-1
Smooth muscle proliferation and medial hypertrophy
Intimal fibrosis and plexiform lesions narrow the lumen
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises

summary: Heart failure means the heart cannot pump enough blood for the body's needs, or can only do so at high filling pressures. Left-sided failure backs blood up into the lungs; right-sided failure backs it up into the body's veins. Know the causes, the compensations that turn harmful, and the classic findings on each side.

points: Main causes: ischemic heart disease, hypertension, aortic and mitral valve disease, cardiomyopathy.
Blood backs up into the pulmonary veins and capillaries and causes pulmonary congestion and edema.
Symptoms: dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea.
Signs: basal crackles, S3, displaced apex beat, pleural effusions.
Lungs show hemosiderin-laden macrophages (heart failure cells) from leaked red cells.
Low forward output reduces kidney perfusion and activates RAAS (prerenal azotemia); low brain perfusion causes confusion.
Most common cause is left-sided heart failure.
Isolated causes: cor pulmonale (lung disease, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary hypertension), right ventricular infarct, tricuspid or pulmonic valve disease.
Blood backs up into the systemic veins: raised JVP, hepatojugular reflux, dependent pitting edema.
Liver: congestive hepatomegaly with nutmeg pattern (centrilobular congestion and necrosis); long-standing cases develop cardiac cirrhosis.
Also ascites, splenomegaly, and pleural and pericardial effusions.
HFrEF: ejection fraction 40% or lower; the ventricle contracts poorly (systolic failure).
HFpEF: ejection fraction 50% or higher; the stiff ventricle fills poorly (diastolic failure).
Ejection fraction 41 to 49% is called mildly reduced.
Frank-Starling: more filling stretches fibers and raises stroke volume until the curve flattens.
Sympathetic activation raises heart rate and contractility but increases O2 demand and arrhythmia risk.
RAAS and ADH retain salt and water, which raises preload and causes edema.
Angiotensin II and aldosterone promote fibrosis and remodeling.
Natriuretic peptides (ANP from atria, BNP from ventricles) are released with stretch and partly oppose RAAS; BNP is a diagnostic marker.
Acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock.
Arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia) and sudden death.
Mural thrombi in dilated chambers that can embolize.
Cardiorenal syndrome and cardiac cachexia.

Pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, arrhythmia, mural thrombus, right heart failure
Left heart failure (most common), cor pulmonale, right ventricular infarct, tricuspid or pulmonic valve disease
Raised JVP, hepatojugular reflux, pitting edema, nutmeg liver, ascites; lungs often clear in pure right failure
Cardiac cirrhosis, ascites, renal congestion, low output

rows: Stiff ventricle, poor relaxation and filling
Hypertension, older age, obesity, diabetes, hypertrophic or restrictive cardiomyopathy

Fails once the curve flattens; congestion

tricks.label: Left goes to the lungs
tricks.text: Left-sided failure backs up into the lungs. Right-sided failure backs up into the rest of the body (neck veins, liver, legs).

tricks.label: S3 floods, S4 stiffens
tricks.text: S3 comes from blood rushing into an overfilled, dilated ventricle. S4 comes from the atrium kicking against a stiff, thick ventricle.

tricks.label: Why orthopnea
tricks.text: Lying flat returns fluid from the legs to the chest, and a failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra volume, so the lungs congest.

highYield: Left heart failure is the most common cause of right heart failure.
Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden macrophages in the alveoli.
Nutmeg liver shows centrilobular congestion from right heart failure.
BNP is released by stretched ventricular myocytes and is used to diagnose heart failure.
Ischemic heart disease is the most common cause of left-sided heart failure.
HFpEF is linked with hypertension and concentric hypertrophy.
pitfalls: Heart failure cells are found in the lungs, not in the heart.
Edema in right heart failure is pitting and dependent; lymphedema and myxedema are nonpitting.
A normal ejection fraction does not rule out heart failure; HFpEF has a normal or high ejection fraction.

Right ventricle fails and systemic venous pressure rises

Dependent pitting edema

Baroreceptors activate sympathetic nerves
Renin release activates angiotensin II and aldosterone
ADH release adds water retention
Salt and water retention raise preload and cause edema

Angiotensin II and aldosterone cause fibrosis and remodeling

summary: Ischemic heart disease happens when coronary blood flow cannot meet myocardial O2 demand, nearly always because of coronary atherosclerosis. It ranges from angina to infarction to slow ischemic heart failure. Expect questions on plaque events, the histologic timeline of an infarct, and which complication appears on which day.

points: Coronary atherosclerosis causes over 90% of cases.
Risk factors: age, male sex, smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high LDL, low HDL, family history, obesity, inactivity.
Other causes: coronary vasospasm, emboli, vasculitis, and high demand states (tachycardia, LVH, severe aortic stenosis).
The subendocardium is most vulnerable because it is last on the coronary supply line and squeezed hardest in systole.
Stable angina: fixed narrowing (about 70% or more) causes chest pain with exertion that eases with rest or nitroglycerin.
Stable angina shows ST depression during pain (subendocardial ischemia).
Unstable angina: plaque disruption with a partial clot causes pain at rest or worsening pain, without troponin rise.
Prinzmetal (variant) angina: coronary vasospasm at rest with transient ST elevation; triggers include smoking and cocaine.
Usual sequence: plaque rupture, platelet adhesion, and a thrombus that blocks the artery.
Irreversible myocyte injury begins after about 20 to 40 minutes of severe ischemia.
Transmural infarct (often STEMI) spans the full wall; subendocardial infarct (often NSTEMI) is limited to the inner third to half.
Artery involved: LAD about 40 to 50%, RCA about 30 to 40%, left circumflex about 15 to 20%.
ECG leads: LAD in V1 to V4, left circumflex in I, aVL, V5, V6, RCA in II, III, aVF.
Troponin rises within about 3 to 4 hours and stays elevated about 7 to 10 days; CK-MB returns to normal in about 2 to 3 days, so it helps detect reinfarction.
Reperfusion injury: contraction band necrosis and free radical damage when flow returns.
Progressive heart failure from ischemic myocardial damage, also called ischemic cardiomyopathy.
Usually follows one or more healed infarcts; scars replace muscle and the remaining muscle hypertrophies.
The left ventricle dilates; diffuse subendocardial myocyte vacuolization and fibrosis are seen.
Complications: progressive heart failure, arrhythmias, sudden cardiac death.

tricks.label: Cells arrive in order
tricks.text: After an MI the cells arrive in the same order as in any acute inflammation: neutrophils first (days 1 to 3), macrophages next (days 3 to 7), then granulation tissue and scar.

tricks.label: Soft wall, rupture risk
tricks.text: Rupture is most likely when macrophages have eaten the dead muscle and no scar has formed yet, roughly days 3 to 14.

tricks.label: Why the posteromedial papillary muscle
tricks.text: The posteromedial papillary muscle usually has a single supply (posterior descending artery), so an inferior MI can rupture it and cause acute mitral regurgitation.

highYield: Ventricular fibrillation is the main cause of death in the first hours after MI.
LAD occlusion is the most common cause of MI and affects the anterior wall and septum.
Contraction band necrosis is a sign of reperfusion.
Free wall rupture causes sudden cardiac tamponade; septal rupture causes a new left-to-right shunt.
Papillary muscle rupture causes acute mitral regurgitation and pulmonary edema.
Dressler syndrome is autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI.
Troponin is the most specific marker of myocyte necrosis.
pitfalls: Unstable angina and NSTEMI both have rest pain; only NSTEMI has a troponin rise.
Stable angina shows ST depression; Prinzmetal angina shows transient ST elevation.
A true ventricular aneurysm is a scarred bulging wall; a pseudoaneurysm is a rupture sealed off by pericardium and has a narrow neck.
Early fibrinous pericarditis (days 1 to 3) comes from the necrosis itself; Dressler syndrome is a later immune reaction.

dumps.p: Draw a timeline from hour 0 to 2 months after an MI. Write the microscopic change and the main complication at each stage.
l: 0 to 4 hours: little visible change; arrhythmia risk highest
4 to 24 hours: coagulative necrosis begins; contraction bands if reperfused
1 to 3 days: neutrophils; fibrinous pericarditis
3 to 7 days: macrophages; rupture risk rises
1 to 2 weeks: granulation tissue
2 weeks to 2 months: collagen scar
Late: ventricular aneurysm, mural thrombus, Dressler syndrome

LAD infarct: V1 to V4
Left circumflex: lateral wall
Left circumflex infarct: I, aVL, V5, V6
RCA: inferior wall, right ventricle, usually SA and AV nodes
RCA infarct: II, III, aVF
Inferior MI can cause bradycardia or AV block and posteromedial papillary muscle rupture

summary: Valve disease either narrows a valve (stenosis, a pressure load) or lets blood leak back (regurgitation, a volume load). The exam links each lesion to its cause, its murmur, and its effect on the chambers, and adds the special valve diseases: endocarditis, MVP, rheumatic heart disease, and carcinoid heart disease.

points: Aortic stenosis: age-related calcification is most common; bicuspid valve causes it at a younger age; rheumatic disease less often.
AS: pressure overload, concentric LVH; syncope, angina, and dyspnea on exertion; weak delayed pulse (pulsus parvus et tardus).
AS can cause hemolysis with schistocytes and GI bleeding from angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome).
Aortic regurgitation: aortic root dilation (hypertension, age, Marfan, syphilis), bicuspid valve, endocarditis, rheumatic disease.
AR: volume overload, eccentric LVH; wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses; acute AR from dissection or endocarditis causes sudden failure.
Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic.
MS raises left atrial pressure: atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, mural thrombi and emboli, pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure.
A large left atrium can compress the esophagus (dysphagia) or the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness).
Mitral regurgitation: MVP, ischemic papillary muscle damage or rupture, left ventricular dilation, rheumatic disease, endocarditis.
MR: volume overload of left atrium and ventricle; S3; atrial fibrillation.
Infective: acute (S. aureus, normal valves, destructive) or subacute (viridans strep, damaged valves, slower).
Mitral valve is involved most often overall; the tricuspid valve in IV drug use.
Nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis: sterile clots on valves in cancer and hypercoagulable states.
Libman-Sacks endocarditis: sterile vegetations on both valve surfaces in lupus.
Signs: fever, new murmur, Janeway lesions (painless, palms and soles), Osler nodes (painful, fingers), Roth spots, splinter hemorrhages.
Myxomatous degeneration: excess proteoglycan in the spongiosa makes leaflets floppy and they balloon into the atrium in systole.
Common (about 2 to 3% of adults); linked to Marfan syndrome, Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, and ADPKD.
Mid-systolic click then a late systolic murmur; standing or Valsalva moves the click earlier.
Usually benign; can lead to mitral regurgitation, endocarditis, arrhythmia, and rarely sudden death.
Rheumatic heart disease: repeated rheumatic fever scars valves; commissures fuse and chordae thicken and shorten.
The mitral valve is affected in nearly all cases; mitral plus aortic is next most common.
Classic chronic result is mitral stenosis with a fish-mouth valve.
Carcinoid heart disease: serotonin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor with liver metastases lets serotonin reach the right heart.
Plaque-like fibrous thickening of the right heart valves and endocardium causes tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis.
The left heart is usually spared because the lungs break down serotonin (monoamine oxidase); urine 5-HIAA is high.

tricks.text: Aortic stenosis symptoms: Syncope, Angina, Dyspnea on exertion.

tricks.label: J♥NES
tricks.text: Major Jones criteria for rheumatic fever: Joints (migratory polyarthritis), heart (carditis), Nodules (subcutaneous), Erythema marginatum, Sydenham chorea.

tricks.label: TIPS
tricks.text: Carcinoid heart disease hits the right side: Tricuspid Insufficiency, Pulmonic Stenosis.

tricks.label: Bacteria FROM JANE
tricks.text: Infective endocarditis signs: Bacteremia, Fever, Roth spots, Osler nodes, Murmur, Janeway lesions, Anemia, Nail-bed (splinter) hemorrhages, Emboli.

highYield: Most common cause of aortic stenosis is age-related calcification; bicuspid valve causes it earlier.
Mitral stenosis is almost always rheumatic.
MVP comes from myxomatous degeneration and is linked to Marfan syndrome.
S. aureus causes acute endocarditis; tricuspid involvement suggests IV drug use.
Carcinoid heart disease needs liver metastases and spares the left heart.
Left atrial enlargement in mitral stenosis leads to atrial fibrillation and stroke.
Standing or Valsalva makes the MVP click earlier and the HCM murmur louder.
pitfalls: Janeway lesions are painless and from septic emboli; Osler nodes are painful and from immune complexes.
Rheumatic fever vegetations are small and sterile; infective endocarditis vegetations are bulky and full of organisms.
Stenosis is a pressure load (concentric hypertrophy); regurgitation is a volume load (eccentric hypertrophy).
The opening snap belongs to mitral stenosis; the mid-systolic click belongs to MVP.
